content: The tuberculosis (TB) clinic is located within the main clinic building and is accessed through a separate entrance. HIV services are provided in a room situated diagonally across from the TB room, and the interior of the HIV room is visible when its doors are open. Patients hand their yellow TB patient cards to the clinic staff through open windows, which are secured with burglar bars. Communication between staff and patients occurs through these open windows, primarily in Kiswahili. The TB nurse, who was the deputy in charge on the day of observation (as the in-charge nurse was absent), reviews the TB register and the patient’s card. Upon entering the facility, patients are weighed in the passageway by a staff member. They then sit on a chair approximately one meter away from the TB nurse for their consultation. Two counselors are also involved in TB services, but they were not present during the initial visit to the facility. A separate patient costing study, led by the World Health Organization (WHO), is ongoing at the facility. A data collector was present in the TB clinic room during the observation. Patients receive their anti-tuberculosis medications weekly, which are pre-packaged in boxes labeled with a unique identifier, such as the patient’s initiation date. These boxes are stored on shelves within the consultation room. The pre-packaging of medications is conducted at a central public dispensary. Daily treatment adherence is monitored at home by either a treatment support partner or a community health care worker. Nutritional support packages, including maize flour and peanut butter, are provided to patients whose body mass index (BMI) falls below 18. Masks are used during the initiation of new patients, although this was not observed as no new patients were seen during the visit. A small laboratory is located outside the clinic, staffed by two laboratory technicians (only one was present during the visit). Microscopy specimens are decontaminated, slides are prepared, and they are examined under an electron microscope (two microscopes are available). A biosafety cabinet with an extraction fan is present in the laboratory, but it was not operational at the time and was scheduled for repair. If the TB nurse requests advanced diagnostic tests such as Xpert® MTB/RIF, culture, drug susceptibility testing (DST), or line probe assays (LPA), the specimens are sent to a nearby facility or a reference laboratory. Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) services are available at the clinic, but cases are rare. The TB nurse had recently managed one MDR-TB patient, who was asked to visit the clinic in the afternoon when fewer patients were present. For patients too ill to attend the clinic, the nurse conducted home visits on foot to minimize exposure risks. Children are also treated for TB at the facility. In the surrounding area, 20 community health care workers, supported by external funding, are assigned to conduct home visits for TB patients. In Romania, a case study was conducted in a hospital laboratory to gather data on the quantities, specifications, and costs of consumables, chemicals, reagents, and equipment used for TB diagnostic tests, including Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) smear microscopy and Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) culture. A senior microbiologist provided detailed information during an interview, which was corroborated by observing the analysis processes. ZN and LJ samples were prepared in batches of 10, requiring a return visit to the laboratory two days later when sufficient samples were available for analysis. The capital costs of equipment used for ZN and LJ tests were calculated by annualizing the purchase price or current market value of the equipment, divided by its life expectancy (using a 3% discount rate). Maintenance costs were added to this value. The mean capital cost per test was determined by dividing the total annualized cost of each piece of equipment by the annual number of tests performed. Recurrent costs, such as utilities, insurance, linens, sterilization, cleaning, security, and general office supplies, were obtained through interviews with the hospital’s financial director. Overhead costs were allocated based on the proportion of laboratory space used for ZN and LJ tests, measured using a tape measure, and divided by the annual number of sputum samples analyzed. In Indonesia, staff costs associated with interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) tests were calculated through interviews with resident doctors and time-motion studies of laboratory technicians. Resident doctors were asked to estimate the time required for patient consultations and IGRA-specific activities, such as explaining the test and drawing blood. Data on monthly working hours, patient volumes, and the number of IGRA tests performed were obtained from the clinic’s lead doctor. In the immunology laboratory, technicians were briefed on the study’s objectives and methodology. They explained the workflow, equipment, and challenges associated with IGRA tests, particularly maintaining blood sample quality during collection, transportation, and analysis. A time-motion study was conducted to capture the time taken for each task, using a digital stopwatch and detailed notes on activities, equipment, and consumables. The study was repeated with a junior technician to calculate an average time for IGRA test analysis. Ethical approval and permission letters were obtained before engaging with clinic and laboratory staff. Informed consent was sought from participants, and all data were anonymized and securely stored. The findings aim to improve TB service delivery and resource planning for national TB programs.
